 Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at Age 67
 Kailey Hagen, CFP®, The Motley Fool 2026년 11월 6일 금 오후 6:20 UTC 0 Image source: Getty Images. Key Points
 As of December 2025, the average benefit for people who are age 67 is $2,016.48 per month.
 A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in 2027, adding about $73 a month to the average age-67 benefit.
 Delayed retirement credits can increase your monthly payment by 8% per year if you wait past your full retirement age to claim.

 As of December 2025 -- the most recent data available -- the average benefit for people aged 67 is $2,016.48 per month, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). For many, this age marks the point where you can claim your full benefit without permanent reductions for early filing.
 Full retirement age (FRA) ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year; 67 is the full retirement age for everyone born in 1960 or later. While 67 is the baseline for younger workers, those who are already 67 today have a full retirement age of 66 years and 10 months. Their current checks might include a small increase for waiting past that baseline.

 The average Social Security benefit at 67
 The SSA tracks how these payments vary across the population. While the combined average is $2,016.48, the data reveals a significant difference between genders. Men at this age receive an average of $2,234.41 per month, while the average benefit among women is $1,801.82.
 That creates a gender gap of $432.59 per month. This difference usually stems from career-long earnings patterns rather than the benefit formula itself. The SSA calculates your benefit based on your highest 35 years of earnings. Those earlier wages are adjusted for inflation and run through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula.

 Beyond the full retirement age baseline
 It's helpful to view your FRA as a neutral baseline rather than a maximum cap. If you wait past 67 to claim, you earn delayed retirement credits . These credits are worth 8% per year, up to age 70. For a worker with a full retirement age of 67, delaying for three years results in a 24% total increase.
 The impact of waiting shows up clearly in the data. The average benefit for 70-year-olds is $2,274.68, which is $258.20 higher than the age-67 average. However, you tend to receive roughly the same total over your lifetime regardless of when you claim, if you live an average lifespan. A later claim simply locks in a higher monthly floor.
 Regardless of your claiming age, your checks will adjust to help protect your purchasing power. A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027, though the figures from December 2025 don't reflect it yet. That adjustment will add about $73 a month on top of the age-67 average to account for rising prices.
 Advertisement
 Even with these increases, Social Security works best as a supplemental source of income. The program was designed to replace only about 40% of pre-retirement income. Most retirees need a much higher share than that to maintain their lifestyle. You'll likely rely on savings or other income sources to bridge the gap.
 When is waiting longer worth it?
 Delaying Social Security beyond your FRA of 67 could lead to a larger lifetime benefit, but you typically must live into your mid-80s or beyond for this to happen. Those with shorter life expectancies often get more from the program by claiming earlier.
 The downside of waiting is that you have to cover your living expenses on your own for a longer period, which might be difficult if you don't have much in personal savings. In that case, applying at your FRA might be a better move than waiting longer, even if it means settling for a smaller lifetime benefit.
 Married individuals should also consider how their decision will affect their spouse before deciding whether to delay Social Security beyond their FRA. Your partner cannot claim a spousal benefit on your work record until you're receiving retirement checks. If they don't qualify for their own retirement benefit, that could be a reason to sign up earlier so you can both begin receiving checks.
